turn_text: Welcome back to Tell Me More, a podcast series featuring distinguished visitors to Tufts University who share their ideas, discuss their work, and shed light on important topics of the day. The week before the death of President George H.W. Senunu reminisces about his time spent with the late President Bush while campaigning for the all-important New Hampshire primary, reflecting on the face-to-face campaign style that he says works so well in his state. He recalls how President Bush met voters over breakfast at McDonald's, Denny's, Dunkin' Donuts, sometimes as many as five restaurants in a single morning. Let's listen in.

turn_text: Today, I am happy to welcome Johnson Unu, a former governor of New Hampshire from 1983 to 1989, and a very interesting piece here, a chief of staff for President George H.W. Bush back in 1989 to 1991. And I want to get right to it. So let's talk about elections, okay? We are looking ahead to these upcoming elections in 2020. How important is New Hampshire?

Well, you can't get to be president if you don't win the New Hampshire primary. And I think there's only one exception to that. So it is important. It is a great process that we have that allows candidates that may not be the candidate of the big money to come in and build up a little bit of a name and a reputation so that they can go elsewhere after doing well in New Hampshire and be supported.
So I wanted to ask you, how does one actually campaign in New Hampshire for a presidential election?

Well, in New Hampshire, a lot of the campaigning is what I call, see me, touch me, feel me campaign. It is face to face. John McCain, for example, had 300 in some odd town meetings where a couple of hundred people would come and he would talk about what he was interested in and walk around afterwards and try and shake his many hands and look as many people in the eye. When George Herbert Walker Bush lost in Iowa, and we had 10 days in New Hampshire to pull it all together for him, I made him go to three, four, five, breakfast every morning. The press thought it was crazy, but he would go to McDonald's, Denny's Dunkin' Donuts and walk around, shake hands with everybody and talk to everybody while they were having a coffee and a donut. It is that personal contact that has to be a significant part of your campaign. It's not everything, but without that, nothing else you do up there will work.

No name that's out there, in my opinion, comes to the top of the pile at this stage. If you ask me who the front runners are, I would say it's Joe Biden and Bernie Sanders, and they're both Dr. Genarians, or almost Dr. Genarians, which is not a good place for the party to be.

So let's reflect back on your stint at the White House as the Chief of Staff for George H.W. Bush. What are your impressions of the United States' current political climate? Compare that to what you saw when you were there in the 80s and 90s.

Well, look, there's always an evolution in process. I have to put it in the context of how presidents communicate. Franklin Roosevelt discovered the radio and went to his fireside chats to go directly to the people. And then John Kennedy discovered network TV, used it brilliantly. Bill Clinton discovered cable TV, tucked his saxophone under his arm and went on all those shows and talked directly to his constituency. Barack Obama was the first to make use of social media. He did it in a broad sense. And now you have Donald Trump discovering that every morning there's 50 million people who wake up to see what the dear leader has tweeted. And so this process of communication has become much more targeted to people. And yet more remote because you're not looking them in the eye. And as a result, I think it's caused much more of a sharpness to occur in the discourse. Everybody can have their own Twitter account and argue with 20,000 people that they've never even seen and be as obnoxious to them as they want and never suffer the response of a tough stare back. And if you're not looking at somebody when you're having this kind of an argument, you tend to be much more obnoxious, much more unwilling to listen to the other side at all and much more willing to come to common discourse. I've said that the problem in the country is not trying to figure out how to come together. The problem in the country is to figure out how we can continue to stand apart, but in a civil manner with civil discord. Of course, we're never going to obliterate differences. We're going to be apart in issues and desires for policy. But what we have to do is not try to figure out how to erase the differences, but how to argue for compromise in a civil way.
